text.en: Look at a plant or tree near your home. Do you see a bird, a butterfly or an ant on it? Many animals, birds and insects live on and around plants. Today we will find out why, and we will also look at the soil under our feet.

Elephants feed on grass, a moth rests on a leaf and a caterpillar chews a leaf. Earthworms live on leaves and in the soil. A tailorbird sings on a tree, a woodpecker sits on a tree trunk, ants build their nest using leaves, and a colourful stink bug sits on a leaf. A frog rests on a leaf, a butterfly perches on a leaf, squirrels use tree hollows to hide and rest, and a barbet uses a tree hollow for nesting. Some of these animals live under the ground too, like earthworms in the soil. We can ask ourselves which of these animals we have seen, and show with our hands and arms how big or small they are.
Animals, birds and insects use different parts of plants for food, shelter and resting. Camels eat the leaves of plants. Monkeys love eating the fruits of plants. Birds like owls use hollows in trees to bring up their young ones. Squirrels and crows use twigs from plants to build their nests. Sunbirds and butterflies drink nectar from different flowers, and tailorbirds stitch the leaves of plants together to build their nests. Bats and leopards use the branches of trees to rest and for shelter, and caterpillars munch on different leaves for food. So plants give animals food, a home and a place to rest, and that is why animals live near them.
Let us stand on the soil next to a plant, with our footwear removed if we are comfortable, and notice the colour of the soil under our feet. We pick up a little soil and look at it. How does it look and feel? It may be dry, damp, rough, smooth, hard or grainy, and we may find leaves, small stones or insects in it. We should also smell the soil and remember its smell. Soil is the topmost layer of the Earth's surface. It is made from rocks broken into tiny pieces, and from old leaves, roots, stems and living and dead animals like insects. On top of the soil, between the grass and leaves, we may find ants, termites, small beetles and grasshoppers. Some of the creatures in soil are too small to see. When it rains and the soil is wet, earthworms and millipedes may come out. We may also find more grasses and plants growing. If we repeat the activity a day after rain, from the same place, we notice differences in look, feel and smell, and soil far from plants is different from soil near plants.
In the monsoons we find many more plants and animals around. They did not come from nowhere. Some insects wait inside the soil for the rains and then come out. Seeds of plants can stay in the soil for a long time and sprout when it rains or when they are watered. That is why we could not see them earlier.
Standing near our plant friend, we look around and spot different animals. We describe each one in words and note where it was and what it was doing. For example: a small hopping insect on the grass jumping around, a black bird, red bugs on a rotting fruit, a blue flying insect, ants on leaves, a butterfly on lantana flowers and a garden lizard on a rock. Watching quietly and carefully helps us notice more.
We close our eyes and listen for bird sounds. We can cup our ears with our hands and face the sound to hear it more clearly. Different birds make different sounds. A pigeon, for example, goes 'gutru gu'. We try making the sounds we heard and write them in a table with the bird name. We can notice whether we hear more sounds in the early morning, afternoon or evening. If we hear no birds, we can think about why.
We can discuss the colour and feel of two soil samples and when we collected them. We can think about which month fresh new leaves appeared on our plant and which animals we noticed near it. Then we write the names of two animals we saw near plants, their shape, size and colours, and guess why they stayed there.

problem.en: Name three ways animals use plants, with one example each.

text.en: Food: a camel eats leaves, a monkey eats fruit, a sunbird drinks nectar.
Shelter: an owl nests in a tree hollow, a tailorbird stitches leaves into a nest.
Resting: bats and leopards rest on branches.

why.en: Branches give a place to rest.

problem.en: How would you describe the soil you picked up?

text.en: Say its colour, and whether it is dry, damp, rough, smooth, hard or grainy.

why.en: Use the touch and sight words from the chapter.

text.en: Say whether you found leaves, small stones or insects.

why.en: Soil is made of many small things.

text.en: Say what it smells like.

why.en: Smell is also a way to observe.

prompt.en: Tell a friend why animals live near plants and what soil is made of.

requiredIdeas.en: Plants give food, shelter and a place to rest
Examples: owl in a tree hollow, caterpillar eating leaves
Soil is the top layer of the Earth made of tiny rock bits, old leaves, roots and tiny animals
Earthworms and ants live in soil

commonMisconceptions.en: Animals live near plants for no reason
Soil has nothing living in it

points.en: Animals, birds and insects use plants for food, shelter and resting.
Soil is the topmost layer of the Earth, made of tiny rock pieces, old leaves, roots, stems and living and dead animals.
Ants, termites, beetles and grasshoppers live on soil; earthworms and millipedes come out in the rain.
Seeds and some insects wait in the soil for rain.
Different birds make different sounds, which we can listen for.
